intro.carita: Uttama Carita (the third episode, chapters 5–13; the Gita Press viniyoga at the head of chapter 5 calls it the uttara-caritra). In the recitation tradition its presiding form is Mahāsarasvatī; this is the Gita Press viniyoga, not a statement of the Purāṇa text. Chapter 8 has no viniyoga of its own in the pāṭha, only a dhyāna: ‘I contemplate Bhavānī, red, her eyes rippling with compassion, her hands holding the noose, the goad, the arrow and the bow, surrounded by rays — the powers beginning with aṇimā — as “I” myself’ (अरुणां करुणातरङ्गिताक्षीं … अहमित्येव विभावये भवानीम्). The same verse, with पुष्पबाणचापाम् ‘the flower-arrow and the bow’ in place of बाणचापहस्ताम्, is the second dhyāna verse of the Lalitā Sahasranāma. The meditation belongs to the liturgy; the chapter itself does not mention it.
intro.summary: Medhas takes up the story (8.1). With Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa slain and their many troops destroyed (8.2), Śumbha, his mind mastered by anger, orders the whole Daitya host to march (8.3): eighty-six clans with weapons raised and eighty-four clans of the Kambus (8.4), fifty Koṭivīrya clans and a hundred of the Dhaumras (8.5), the Kālakas, Daurhṛdas, Mauryas and Kālakeyas (8.6); and for the first time he sets out himself, with many thousands of troops (8.7). Seeing him come, Caṇḍikā fills the space between earth and sky with the twang of her bowstring (8.8); the lion roars, and Ambikā swells the roar with her bell (8.9); Kālī, her mouth gaping, outdoes all three sounds with her own (8.10). The Daitya armies close in on the Goddess, the lion and Kālī (8.11). At that moment, to destroy the gods’ enemies, the Śaktis of Brahmā, Śiva, Skanda, Viṣṇu and Indra leave their gods’ bodies and come to Caṇḍikā, each with her god’s form, ornaments and mount (8.12–14): Brahmāṇī in a swan-drawn car with rosary and water-pot (8.15), Māheśvarī on the bull with trident, serpent bracelets and crescent moon (8.16), Kaumārī with spear and peacock (8.17), Vaiṣṇavī on Garuḍa with conch, discus, mace, bow and sword (8.18), Vārāhī in the body of the Sacrificial Boar (8.19), Nārasiṃhī, whose tossing mane scatters the stars (8.20), and Aindrī, thunderbolt in hand, on the king of elephants, thousand-eyed (8.21). Śiva, surrounded by them, asks Caṇḍikā to slay the asuras at once (8.22). From the Goddess’s own body comes forth her Śakti, howling like a hundred jackals (8.23), and sends Śiva himself as her messenger to Śumbha and Niśumbha (8.24–25): let Indra have the three worlds and the gods their offerings, and let the asuras go to Pātāla if they wish to live — or come and feed her jackals (8.26–27). So she is known as Śivadūtī (8.28). The asuras march in indignation to where Kātyāyanī stands (8.29) and rain weapons on her (8.30); she cuts them down as if in play (8.31). Kālī ranges at the front with spear and skull-staff (8.32); Brahmāṇī saps the enemy with water from her pot (8.33); Māheśvarī, Vaiṣṇavī and Kaumārī strike with trident, discus and spear (8.34); Aindrī’s thunderbolt fells them in hundreds (8.35); Vārāhī gores them with snout and tusks (8.36); Nārasiṃhī tears them with her claws and devours them (8.37); Śivadūtī fells them with her laughter and eats them (8.38). The asura soldiers slip away (8.39), and Raktabīja advances (8.40): whenever a drop of his blood falls to the ground, an asura of his own stature springs up (8.41). Aindrī’s thunderbolt draws his blood (8.42), and warriors with his form and strength rise from every drop and fight the Mothers (8.43–45); a second stroke yields thousands (8.46); Vaiṣṇavī’s discus and Aindrī’s mace (8.47) fill the world with his doubles (8.48); Kaumārī, Vārāhī and Māheśvarī strike him (8.49), he strikes back at each Mother with his mace (8.50), and from every wound hundreds more arise (8.51), until the whole world is overrun and the gods are seized with fear (8.52). Caṇḍikā tells Kālī — Cāmuṇḍā — to open her mouth wide (8.53), to catch the blood her weapons draw and the asuras born of it (8.54), and to range the field devouring them, so that, drained of blood, he will perish (8.55–56); then she strikes him with her spear (8.56). Kālī takes his blood in her mouth; his mace-blow on Caṇḍikā (8.57) causes her not the slightest pain, while his blood pours out (8.58). Cāmuṇḍā catches it wherever it flows, eats the asuras born in her mouth and drinks his blood (8.59–60), and the Goddess strikes him down with spear, thunderbolt, arrows, swords and blades; he falls, bloodless (8.60–62). The gods rejoice beyond measure, and the band of Mothers born from them dances, wild with blood (8.62–63).
intro.forms: Caṇḍikā (चण्डिका, 8.8, 8.13, 8.22, 8.53, 8.57), the Goddess at the centre of the battle, also Ambikā (8.9), the Devī (8.11, 8.30, 8.56, 8.60), Kātyāyanī (8.29) and ‘the Unconquered’ (अपराजिता, 8.24); Kālī (8.10, 8.11, 8.32, 8.53, 8.57), called by her name of chapter 7, Cāmuṇḍā (8.53, 8.59, 8.60, 8.61), the mouth that drinks Raktabīja’s blood; the Śaktis of the gods, each in her god’s likeness (8.13–14): Brahmāṇī (8.15, 8.33), Māheśvarī (8.16, 8.34, 8.49), Kaumārī — called अम्बिका गुहरूपिणी, ‘the Mother in the form of Guha’ (8.17) — Vaiṣṇavī (8.18, 8.34, 8.47), Vārāhī (8.19, 8.36, 8.49), Nārasiṃhī (8.20, 8.37) and Aindrī (8.21, 8.35, 8.42, 8.47), together ‘the band of Mothers’ (मातृगण, 8.39, 8.40, 8.63); and Caṇḍikā’s own Śakti, howling like a hundred jackals, named Śivadūtī because she made Śiva her messenger (8.23, 8.28, 8.38). Bhavānī, of the dhyāna, is the form of the liturgy, not of the text.
intro.significance: This is the third and greatest of the forces sent against the Devī after Dhūmralocana (chapter 6) and Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa (chapter 7): not a general and his army but the whole Daitya host, with Śumbha himself at its head (8.3–7), though he does not meet her until chapter 9. The chapter brings two new things into the war. First, the Mothers: the powers of the gods leave their bodies and fight for Caṇḍikā in the gods’ own likeness (8.13–14). The text here calls them the gods’ śaktis; only later does the Goddess tell Śumbha that all these powers are hers and take them back into herself (10.5–6). Second, an enemy whom wounding only multiplies (8.41): every Mother’s blow fills the world with more Raktabījas (8.43–52), and the battle the Mothers are winning becomes the gods’ fear. The turn is not a stronger weapon but Cāmuṇḍā’s mouth (8.53–61), the devouring power born in chapter 7 (7.9–13), which catches the blood before it reaches the ground. Between the two stands Śivadūtī, the Goddess’s own Śakti, who makes Śiva himself her envoy (8.24–28) and offers the asuras peace on the gods’ terms (8.26–27).
intro.grammar: A narrative chapter of perfects — reduplicated (आदिदेश, निर्जगाम, ययुः, आययौ, जघान, चिच्छेद, चचार, चखाद, सुस्राव, समुत्तस्थुः, ववाह, जगृहे, पपौ, पपात, ननर्त), the unreduplicated पेतुः and नेशुः (8.35, 8.39), the ātmanepada युयुधे beside the epic युयुधुः (8.42, 8.45), and the periphrastic पूरयामास, ताडयामास (8.8, 8.47) — beside imperfects (व्यचरत्, अकरोत्, न्यपतन्, अताडयत्), one without its augment (उपबृंहयत्, 8.9) and one epic thematic form (अहनत्, 8.50). Past participles stand for finite verbs at each arrival (आयाता, प्राप्ता, विनिष्क्रान्ता, 8.15–23). Commands come in three persons: Śumbha’s third-person imperatives to absent troops (निर्यान्तु, निर्गच्छन्तु, 8.4–6), Śiva’s passive imperative (हन्यन्ताम्, 8.22), and the Goddess’s second-person orders (गच्छ, ब्रूहि, 8.24–25; आगच्छत, 8.27; कुरु, प्रतीच्छ, चर, 8.53–55). The chapter is built on correlatives: locative absolutes (8.2), यस्य … यद्रूपम् … तद्वत् (8.14), यतः … ततः (8.28), येन येन … स्म (8.33), यदा … तदा (8.41), यावन्तः … तावन्तः (8.44). The Mothers’ names are vṛddhi derivatives with the feminine -ī (माहेश्वरी, कौमारी, वैष्णवी, वाराही, नारसिंही, ऐन्द्री) or -ānī (ब्रह्माणी). Sentences run across verses at 8.2–3, 8.12–13, 8.59–60, 8.60–61 and 8.61–62.
intro.teaching: Literally, the gods’ powers come out of their bodies to fight beside the Goddess, an asura whose every drop of blood becomes another asura fills the world with his doubles, and Kālī drinks his blood so that he can be killed. As teaching, the chapter shows the one power acting in many forms: each Mother is a god’s power in that god’s shape (8.14), yet Kaumārī is called simply ‘the Mother’ (8.17), and the tradition, following 10.5–6, reads all of them as the Devī’s own. In the Śākta reading Śiva’s errand (8.24–28) shows the god acting at the bidding of Śakti; that is a reading of the tradition, not a statement of the verse, which says only that she sent him and so won her name. Raktabīja is often read today as a picture of desire or habit that grows every time it is fought on its own terms; that reading is modern. What the verses themselves say is plain: striking him harder only multiplied him (8.43–52), and he died when his blood was received before it touched the ground (8.54–61).
themes: The Mothers: the gods’ powers in the gods’ forms
Śivadūtī: the Goddess who sends Śiva
Raktabīja: an enemy multiplied by every wound
Cāmuṇḍā’s mouth: ending the source, not the copies
Battle in sound before battle in arms

conclusion.narrative: Śumbha, having lost his generals, sends the whole Daitya host and goes with it. The Goddess answers first with sound, then with company: the powers of Brahmā, Śiva, Skanda, Viṣṇu and Indra come to her in their gods’ forms, and her own Śakti sends Śiva to the asuras with the gods’ terms. The Mothers rout the host, but Raktabīja, whose blood becomes asuras wherever it falls, turns every blow into more enemies until the gods despair. Caṇḍikā’s answer is Cāmuṇḍā’s open mouth: the blood is drunk, the doubles are eaten, and Raktabīja falls, drained. The chapter ends with the Mothers’ dance (8.63); the brothers themselves are still to come (chapter 9).

constructions: The perfect as the narrative past, including the unreduplicated पेतुः, नेशुः (8.35, 8.39) and the periphrastic पूरयामास, ताडयामास (8.8, 8.47).
Third-person imperatives for commands to the absent (निर्यान्तु, 8.4; लभताम्, सन्तु, 8.26) and a passive imperative (हन्यन्ताम्, 8.22).
Relative–correlative pairs that carry the logic of the chapter: यस्य … यत् … तद्वत् (8.14), यदा … तदा (8.41), यावन्तः … तावन्तः (8.44), यतः … ततः (8.28).
The present for a standing fact (पतति, 8.41) and for past narrative (धावति स्म, 8.33; सम्प्रतीच्छति, 8.59).
One singular verb for several subjects, each with her own instrument (जघान, 8.34, 8.49).
Vṛddhi taddhitas forming the Mothers’ names (माहेश्वरी, वैष्णवी, ऐन्द्री, नारसिंही), with ब्रह्माणी in -ānī.
Epic (ārṣa) forms kept as printed: युयुधुः (8.45), अहनत् (8.50), उत्पत्स्यन्ति (8.56), जिग्ये (8.10).
Hiatus at the pāda break, printed so in the Gita Press: निर्यान्तु | आज्ञया (8.6), ताडयामास | ऐन्द्री (8.47).
insights: The gods’ powers are feminine and can act without their gods: the Śaktis leave the gods’ bodies and fight in their likeness while the gods look on (8.13–14, 8.22).

Each Mother is the one Mother in a particular form: Kaumārī is called अम्बिका (8.17), and the Mothers are named as one band (8.39, 8.63); at 10.5–6 the Goddess claims them as her own and takes them back into herself.
The Goddess sends the highest god as her envoy (8.24), and the name she earns, Śivadūtī, records it (8.28).
Her terms are restoration, not destruction: Indra’s rule, the gods’ offerings, and life for the asuras in Pātāla (8.26).
Some enemies grow with every blow: the Mothers’ weapons multiply Raktabīja (8.43–52), and he dies only when his blood is received before it reaches the ground (8.53–61).
conclusion.srividya: The one specific connection is liturgical, not in the Purāṇa text: the Gita Press dhyāna before this chapter is, with one change of wording (बाणचापहस्ताम् for पुष्पबाणचापाम्), the second dhyāna verse of the Lalitā Sahasranāma — red Bhavānī with noose, goad, bow and arrow, surrounded by the powers beginning with aṇimā, contemplated as ‘I’. The Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) names the same four weapons (8, रागस्वरूपपाशाढ्या; 9, क्रोधाकाराङ्कुशोज्ज्वला; 10, मनोरूपेक्षुकोदण्डा; 11, पञ्चतन्मात्रसायका) and the name Bhavānī (112, भवानी). In Śrīvidyā worship eight Mothers (Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, Māhendrī, Cāmuṇḍā, Mahālakṣmī) are honoured in the outer square of the Śrīcakra; the list overlaps with this chapter’s Mothers but belongs to a separate liturgical tradition. Several names of the chapter are also names in the Lalitā Sahasranāma: Caṇḍikā (755, चण्डिका), Ambikā (295, अम्बिका), Kātyāyanī (556, कात्यायनी), Śivadūtī (405, शिवदूती), Māheśvarī (208, माहेश्वरी) and Vaiṣṇavī (892, वैष्णवी), there names of the supreme Goddess, and Brāhmī (675, ब्राह्मी), a different form from Brahmāṇī; Vārāhī appears there in another battle (76, विशुक्रप्राणहरणवाराहीवीर्यनन्दिता), and Mahākālī, Mahāgrāsā and Mahāśanā (751–753, महाकाली, महाग्रासा, महाशना) name in general terms the devouring power Cāmuṇḍā shows here. These are shared Śākta names, not evidence that one text depends on the other; the chapter itself states no specifically Śrīvidyā doctrine.

key_verses.why: The Śaktis of Brahmā, Śiva, Skanda, Viṣṇu and Indra leave their bodies and go to Caṇḍikā.
Whatever form, ornaments and mount each god had, in just that form his Śakti came to fight.
Because she made Śiva himself her messenger, she became known in the world as Śivadūtī.
Whenever a drop of Raktabīja’s blood falls to the ground, an asura of his stature springs up from the earth.
Seeing the gods in despair, Caṇḍikā tells Kālī: ‘Cāmuṇḍā, open your mouth wide.’
The Goddess strikes down Raktabīja, whose blood Cāmuṇḍā has drunk, and he falls to the ground.
The band of Mothers born from the gods dances, wild with blood: the chapter’s last half-verse.

sandhi_patterns: -aḥ before voiced consonants → -o (शुम्भो भैरवशासनः, क्रुद्धो रक्तबीजो महासुरः), and before a → -o with avagraha (गदापातोऽल्पिकाम्, ततोऽसौ, शतशोऽसुराः); pūrvarūpa after -e as well (तेऽपि, येऽस्याः).

-āḥ before a voiced sound → -ā (कालका दौर्हृदा मौर्याः, पुरुषा जाताः); visarga → r before vowels and voiced consonants (ऋषिरुवाच, सहस्रैर्बहुभिर्वृतः); visarga → s/ś before t/c (सिंहस्तथा, पुनश्च); सः and एषः lose their visarga (स पपात, एवमेष क्षयम्).
Final n before c/t/ś: n → ṃś/ṃs and ñ (विदारितांश्चान्यान्, पतितांस्तान्, बाणाञ्छूल-, आसञ्छतशः); n before j → ñ (दैत्याञ्जघान); t + ś → cch (चाकरोच्छत्रून्, मच्छिवाः, मच्छस्त्र-).
t/d voiced before voiced sounds (तद्वदेव, चेद्भवन्तः, शरीराद्रक्त-) and assimilated before n (तन्नादम्, रक्तपातान्महासुराः).
Savarṇa-dīrgha, guṇa, vṛddhi and yaṇ across words (ममाज्ञया, चोपबृंहयत्, तथैवैन्द्री, क्षयितेष्वसुरेश्वरः); ayādi in दानवावतिगर्वितौ and असावाजघान.
Two declared hiatuses at the pāda break: निर्यान्तु | आज्ञया (8.6) and ताडयामास | ऐन्द्री (8.47).
samasa: Bahuvrīhis of description throughout the Mothers’ portraits (साक्षसूत्रकमण्डलुः, महाहिवलया, मयूरवरवाहना, वज्रहस्ता, सहस्रनयना, सटाक्षेपक्षिप्तनक्षत्रसंहतिः) and of Raktabīja (रक्तबीजः, तत्प्रमाणः, तद्रूपाः, क्षीणरक्तः, नीरक्तः, चामुण्डापीतशोणितम्).

Tṛtīyā tatpuruṣas of means and agent in the battle (शूलपातविदारितान्, खट्वाङ्गपोथितान्, तुण्डप्रहारविध्वस्ताः, शिवदूत्यभिदूषिताः, शस्त्रसङ्घसमाहतः) and pañcamī tatpuruṣas of origin (असुरासृक्सम्भूतैः, मच्छस्त्रपातसम्भूतान्, तदुत्पन्नान्).

Ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣas of possession and rule (असुरेश्वरः, तच्छक्तिः, चण्डिकाशक्तिः, रक्तबिन्दुः, ऐन्द्रीकुलिशपातेन) and upapada tatpuruṣas with agent nouns (सुरद्विषाम्, हविर्भुजः, त्रिशूलवरधारिणी, शिवाशतनिनादिनी).

Itaretara dvandvas of names and weapons (ब्रह्मेशगुहविष्णूनाम्, शङ्खचक्रगदाशार्ङ्गखड्ग-, शूलशक्तिपरश्वधान्, दैत्यदानवाः), a samāhāra dvandva (भूषणवाहनम्), numeral compounds (षडशीतिः, चतुरशीतिः) and prādi compounds with अति (अतिभीषणा, अत्युग्रा, अतिकोपना).
grammar_notes: Several sentences run across verses: 8.2–3, 8.12–13, 8.59–60, 8.60–61 and 8.61–62; the anvayas say so.
आयान्तम् (8.8) is read strictly as masculine, of Śumbha who set out in 8.7, not loosely of the army.
जिग्ये (8.10) is taken as active ‘outdid’, supported by 9.22 and 9.26; परिवारिताः (8.11) is feminine though the lion is among its subjects.
Epic forms are kept and explained: augmentless उपबृंहयत् (8.9), parasmaipada युयुधुः (8.45) and उत्पत्स्यन्ति (8.56), thematic अहनत् (8.50).
प्राहसत्वरा (8.53) is divided प्राह सत्वरा; रक्तबिन्दोः (8.54) is read as an ablative, not a name; तद्वक्त्रेण (8.59) as two words, तत् + वक्त्रेण.
शक्ति keeps both senses in the chapter: the gods’ powers (8.13) and Skanda’s spear (8.17, 8.34).
themes: The Mothers as the gods’ powers
uncertain: 8.41: तत्प्रमाणस्तदासुरः (Gita Press) / तत्प्रमाणो महासुरः (GRETIL, Freund) — Textual Verification Required; the Gita Press reading is kept, and the sense is the same.
8.47: Aindrī strikes with a mace (गदया), though her weapon elsewhere in the chapter is the thunderbolt; no variant is recorded, and the text is translated as written.

Interpretive doubts, none about the reading, are flagged on 8.4 (उदायुधाः as epithet or clan name; the noun counted), 8.8 (आयान्तम् of Śumbha or of the army), 8.10 (the construction of जिग्ये), 8.32 (whose front तस्य अग्रतः means), 8.37 (अन्यान् with विदारितान् or apart), 8.39 (नेशुः ‘fled’ or ‘perished’), 8.53 (the division of प्राहसत्वरा), 8.54 (रक्तबिन्दोः as ablative or a name), 8.59 (तद्वक्त्रेण as one word or two) and 8.63 (the construction of तेषाम्).

In recitation this mantra carries the bīja ॐ, which belongs to the pāṭha, not to the verse.

comm.t: A summary of chapter 7: Caṇḍa was beheaded (7.20), Muṇḍa felled (7.21), and their army was destroyed or fled (7.22). Each word for the deaths is a past participle; the defeat is stated as already complete.

The narrative pattern of the third carita is escalation: one general (Dhūmralocana, ch. 6), then two (Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa, ch. 7), now the whole host. Each defeat draws out a greater manifestation of the Goddess.

mantras.lit: then Śumbha, the mighty, his mind dependent on anger, ordered the setting out of the Daityas, of all the troops.
mantras.tr: — Śumbha, the mighty, his mind wholly mastered by anger, ordered all the Daitya armies to march.

comm.t: Śumbha answers the loss of Caṇḍa and Muṇḍa with a total mobilization. The narrator stresses that the order comes from a mind not its own master (पराधीन).

Through the Śumbha cycle the asura king acts from pride and anger (6.3 सक्रोधः, here कोपपराधीनचेताः), never from counsel; the tradition reads the asuras as passions that grow stronger the more they are opposed.
A modern reflection: the compound’s own word for Śumbha’s state is पराधीन, ‘dependent on another’. The mighty king is, in that moment, not free; anger has taken the throne.

mantras.lit: Today let the Daityas, eighty-six, with weapons raised, (go forth) with all their forces; let eighty-four of the Kambus go forth, surrounded by their own forces.
mantras.tr: “Today let the eighty-six Daitya clans march out with all their forces, weapons raised, and the eighty-four clans of the Kambus, each surrounded by its own troops.
mantras.tr_note: What is counted is not named; ‘clans’ is supplied from कुलानि in 8.5. The plural वृताः is construed with the eighty-four by sense.

comm.t: Śumbha’s command begins (8.4–6). He names asura clans by number; the list conveys the size of the host rather than an order of battle.
The Kambus and the clans of 8.5–6 belong to the Purāṇic lore of the asura races; the text names them once and does not describe them again.

mantras.tr: Let the fifty asura clans of the Koṭivīryas, and the hundred clans of the Dhaumras, march out at my command.
mantras.tr_note: ‘and’ is supplied between the two subjects.

comm.t: The muster continues: fifty Koṭivīrya clans and a hundred Dhaumra clans. The phrase मम आज्ञया makes the order personal; it returns in the next verse.

Dhaumra is formed from Dhūmra, ‘smoke-coloured’, the word that named Dhūmralocana (‘Smoke-eye’), slain by a mere हुंकार of Ambikā (6.13). Whether the text means his kin is not stated; the name may simply mark another asura line.

sandhi_exceptions.reason: Hiatus at the pāda boundary: निर्यान्तु closes the third pāda and आज्ञया opens the fourth. Joining them (निर्यान्त्वाज्ञया) would erase the pāda break; the verse, like much epic and Purāṇic verse, leaves vowels unjoined across a pāda boundary (a metrical licence). The Gita Press text prints them apart.

mantras.tr: Let the Kālakas, the Daurhṛdas, the Mauryas and the Kālakeyas — every asura — march out at once at my command, armed for battle.”
mantras.tr_note: तथासुराः is rendered as summing up the list (‘every asura’); it may also mean ‘and the other asuras’.

comm.t: The muster ends with four more asura clans and the repeated मम आज्ञया. The haste (त्वरिताः) matches Śumbha’s anger in 8.3.

The Kālakeyas are known from the Mahābhārata: they are the asuras who hide in the ocean until Agastya drinks it dry, and Arjuna later fights them with the Paulomas. The Devī Māhātmya draws its enemies from the same old lineages of the asuras.

mantras.anvaya: चण्डिका आयान्तं (शुम्भम्) अतिभीषणं तत्सैन्यं (च) दृष्ट्वा ज्यास्वनैः धरणीगगनान्तरं पूरयामास।
mantras.anvaya_en: An absolutive clause with two objects (आयान्तम्, तत्सैन्यम्), then the main verb पूरयामास with its instrument and object.
mantras.lit: Caṇḍikā, having seen (him) approaching, and his exceedingly terrible army, filled the space between earth and sky with the twangs of her bowstring.
mantras.tr: Seeing Śumbha approach with his dreadful army, Caṇḍikā filled the space between earth and sky with the twanging of her bowstring.
mantras.tr_note: ‘Śumbha’ is supplied from the masculine participle आयान्तम्; see Samāsa.

comm.t: The Goddess answers the muster with sound before any weapon is loosed. The bowstring’s twang filling heaven and earth recalls her first battle, where the same sound shook the underworlds (2.38, धनुर्ज्यानिःस्वनेन).
Caṇḍikā is also a name in the Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa), name 755, चण्डिका. In the Devī Māhātmya it is the commonest name of the Goddess in battle.

flags.uncertain: आयान्तम् is masculine; most renderings take it loosely with the army (‘seeing that army approaching’). The analysis reads it strictly, of Śumbha, who set out in 8.7.

samasa.sense: with the clanging of her bell

samasa.alt: Not two words: a separate तत् is neuter and could not agree with the masculine नादम्.

morph.note: The past active participle (-तवत्) is often used for a finite past: सिंहः … कृतवान् ‘the lion made’.
The regular imperfect would be उपाबृंहयत् (the augment अ stands between prefix and verb). The augmentless form is an epic licence (or an injunctive with past sense); the meaning is unaffected.
Vocative: Medhas addresses King Suratha, his listener.

mantras.anvaya: नृप, ततः सिंहः अतीव महानादं कृतवान्; अम्बिका च घण्टास्वनेन तन्नादम् उपबृंहयत्।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two clauses joined by च: the lion’s roar, and Ambikā’s bell amplifying it.
mantras.lit: Then the lion made an exceedingly great roar, O king, and Ambikā swelled that roar of his with the sound of her bell.
mantras.tr: Then, O king, the lion gave a mighty roar, and Ambikā swelled that roar with the clanging of her bell.

comm.t: The second and third sounds join the bowstring of 8.8: the lion’s roar and the bell. Ambikā and Caṇḍikā are the same Goddess under two names.

The bell was Indra’s gift, taken from Airāvata (2.22); in the first battle its sound bewildered the asuras (2.56), and the gods pray to be guarded by it (4.24; 11.27). Its sound is itself a weapon that weakens the enemy.

samasa.type: bahuvrīhi (containing a tṛtīyā relation नादेन आपूरित and a ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa दिङ्मुख)

samasa.sense: Kālī amid the din that fills every direction
samasa.alt: As in 7.8, where the same epithet describes Kālī, it can mean ‘she by whom the quarters are filled with sound’ (नादेन आपूरितानि दिङ्मुखानि यया सा). Here the sound is said to be that of the bowstring, lion and bell, which are not Kālī’s, so the looser ‘around whom’ is chosen. The genitive धनुर्ज्यासिंहघण्टानाम् is construed with the member नाद- (an epic licence).

samasa.literal: she by whom the mouth is stretched wide

morph.note: Perfect of √जि with an ātmanepada ending. √जि is parasmaipada (जिगाय); जिग्ये could formally be a passive perfect (‘was conquered’), but with काली as subject and the instrumental निनादैः the sense is active: ‘she prevailed (over those sounds) with her roars’.
विस्तारित is the past participle of the causative of वि + √स्तृ ‘to spread’: ‘made wide’.

mantras.anvaya: धनुर्ज्यासिंहघण्टानां नादापूरितदिङ्मुखा विस्तारितानना काली भीषणैः निनादैः जिग्ये।
mantras.anvaya_en: The subject काली carries two bahuvrīhis; the verb जिग्ये has the instrument भीषणैः निनादैः. What she outdid — the sounds just named — is understood.
mantras.lit: Kālī — the faces of the quarters about her filled with the sound of bowstring, lion and bell — her mouth stretched wide, prevailed with terrible roars.
mantras.tr: With the twang of the bow, the lion’s roar and the clang of the bell filling every quarter, Kālī, her mouth gaping wide, outdid them all with her terrible roars.
mantras.tr_note: The object of ‘outdid’ (the three sounds) is supplied; जिग्ये is taken in its active sense.

comm.t: The fourth sound, Kālī’s roar, tops the other three. Both epithets repeat her portrait at her birth (7.8: नादापूरितदिङ्मुखा, अतिविस्तारवदना).

Before the armies close, the battle is fought in sound. The scene returns at Śumbha’s own onset (9.19–22): conch, bowstring, bell and lion fill the quarters, then Kālī strikes earth and sky and ‘the earlier sounds were drowned out’ (प्राक्स्वनास्ते तिरोहिताः, 9.22). At 9.26 √जि is again used of one sound overcoming another (जितवान्), which supports the reading of जिग्ये here.

flags.uncertain: The construction is loose: the genitive धनुर्ज्यासिंहघण्टानाम् hangs on the member नाद- of a compound, and जिग्ये is an ātmanepada perfect of a parasmaipada root. The reading ‘Kālī outdid those sounds with her roars’ is supported by the parallel at 9.22 and 9.26; ‘Kālī, who filled the quarters with the sound …, prevailed with her roars’ is also possible.

morph.note: The participle is feminine plural although the lion is masculine. Strict grammar lets the masculine prevail in a mixed group; the feminine here follows the two goddesses who head the list (an epic licence of agreement).
In a passive sentence the absolutive goes with the agent in the instrumental: it is the Daitya armies who heard the roar and then surrounded the three.

mantras.anvaya: तं निनादम् उपश्रुत्य सरोषैः दैत्यसैन्यैः देवी सिंहः तथा काली चतुर्दिशं परिवारिताः (आसन्)।
mantras.anvaya_en: A passive sentence: the subjects (देवी, सिंहः, काली) with the participle परिवारिताः; the agent दैत्यसैन्यैः also does the hearing (उपश्रुत्य).
mantras.lit: Having heard that roar, by the enraged Daitya armies on four sides the Goddess, the lion and also Kālī were surrounded.
mantras.tr: Hearing that roar, the furious Daitya armies closed in on every side around the Goddess, the lion and Kālī.
mantras.tr_note: The passive is turned into an active sentence.

comm.t: The din draws the whole enemy host in, and the three — the Goddess, her lion and Kālī — are encircled. The situation is set for the help that arrives in the next verse.

The three on the Goddess’s side are the Goddess, her mount and Kālī, the power that sprang from her own brow (7.6). The Mothers who now join them are a further multiplication of the one power facing the many.

mantras.anvaya: भूप, एतस्मिन् अन्तरे सुरद्विषां विनाशाय अमरसिंहानां भवाय (च) अतिवीर्यबलान्विताः (शक्तयः …)
mantras.anvaya_en: Time, vocative, two datives of purpose, and an adjective waiting for its noun (शक्तयः) and verb (ययुः) in 8.13.
mantras.lit: At this juncture, O king, for the destruction of the enemies of the gods (and) for the well-being of the lion-like immortals, endowed with surpassing valour and strength —
mantras.tr: At that very moment, O king, to destroy the enemies of the gods and for the good of the foremost of the immortals, (powers) endowed with surpassing valour and might —
mantras.tr_note: The noun the adjective qualifies (‘powers’) is supplied from 8.13.

comm.t: The purpose is stated before the actors appear: the śaktis come to destroy the asuras and to secure the gods. The vocative भूप reminds us that Medhas is telling this to Suratha.
The paired datives — destruction of the hostile, welfare of the good — follow the familiar formula of divine descent, as in the Bhagavadgītā (4.8: परित्राणाय साधूनां विनाशाय च दुष्कृताम्).

mantras.anvaya_en: The subject promised in 8.12 (शक्तयः) with its genitives, an absolutive of motion out of the gods’ bodies, and the main verb ययुः with its goal चण्डिकाम्.
mantras.lit: — the Śaktis of Brahmā, Īśa, Guha and Viṣṇu, and likewise of Indra, having come forth from their bodies, went to Caṇḍikā with their forms.
mantras.tr: — the Śaktis of Brahmā, Śiva, Skanda and Viṣṇu, and of Indra too, came forth from their bodies and went to Caṇḍikā, each in the form of her god.
mantras.tr_note: Īśa and Guha are rendered by their familiar names, Śiva and Skanda; ‘each in the form of her god’ interprets तद्रूपैः in the light of 8.14.

comm.t: The powers of five gods leave their bodies and join Caṇḍikā. As in chapter 2, where the Goddess took shape from the radiance of all the gods, the divine power leaves the gods and gathers in her.

These are the Mothers (मातृगण, 8.39): Brahmāṇī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, Nārasiṃhī and Aindrī, introduced one by one in 8.15–21. Vārāhī and Nārasiṃhī are Viṣṇu’s further forms; the gods are five but the Mothers seven.

In Śrīvidyā worship eight Mothers — Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, Kaumārī, Vaiṣṇavī, Vārāhī, Māhendrī, Cāmuṇḍā and Mahālakṣmī — are worshipped in the outer square (bhūpura) of the Śrīcakra. The list overlaps with this chapter’s Mothers but belongs to a separate liturgical tradition.

mantras.anvaya_en: A relative–correlative sentence: यत् … यथा … are answered by तद्वत् एव; the main clause is तच्छक्तिः … आययौ.
mantras.lit: Of whichever god whatever was the form, and as (were his) ornaments and vehicle, just so indeed his Śakti came to fight the asuras.
mantras.tr: Whatever form each god had, whatever his ornaments and his mount, in just that form his Śakti came to fight the asuras.

comm.t: The rule for all that follows: each Śakti has her god’s form, insignia and mount. Verses 8.15–21 apply it one by one.
In Śākta thought the god acts only through his Śakti. Here the Śaktis come without their gods and fight in their likeness — the power, not its bearer, takes the field.

samasa.literal: at the front of the swan-yoked car

samasa.vigraha: अक्षसूत्रेण कमण्डलुना च सह वर्तते या सा (अक्षसूत्रम् = अक्षाणां सूत्रम्)
samasa.literal: she who is with rosary and water-pot
samasa.sense: bearing Brahmā’s rosary and ascetic’s water-pot

morph.note: Feminine of ब्रह्मन् with the augment -आन- and -ई (as इन्द्राणी from इन्द्र, रुद्राणी from रुद्र): ‘the consort or power of Brahmā’.
Passive present of अभि + √धा: the root vowel becomes ī before the passive -य- (धीयते). ‘Is named’, with the name in the nominative.
A bahuvrīhi ending in a u-stem keeps that stem in the feminine: nominative -उः, not -ऊ.

mantras.anvaya: हंसयुक्तविमानाग्रे साक्षसूत्रकमण्डलुः ब्रह्मणः शक्तिः आयाता; सा ब्रह्माणी (इति) अभिधीयते।
mantras.anvaya_en: Two clauses: the arrival (शक्तिः आयाता, with place and attributes), then the name (सा ब्रह्माणी अभिधीयते).
mantras.lit: At the front of a car yoked with swans, with rosary and water-pot, came the Śakti of Brahmā; she is called Brahmāṇī.
mantras.tr: Brahmā’s Śakti came seated in a chariot drawn by swans, bearing a rosary and a water-pot. She is called Brahmāṇī.

comm.t: The first of the Mothers mirrors Brahmā: the swan-drawn car, the rosary and the water-pot. Her water-pot becomes a weapon when the battle begins (8.33).
The gods praise her in this form in chapter 11 (11.13: हंसयुक्तविमानस्थे ब्रह्माणीरूपधारिणि), and at 10.6 the Mothers, ‘with Brahmāṇī at their head’ (ब्रह्माणीप्रमुखाः), return into the one Goddess.

The Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) names the Goddess ब्राह्मी (name 675), the other form of the same feminine of Brahmā. The two texts use different forms; the identity is of idea, not of wording.

morph.note: Vṛddhi of the first syllable (म → मा) forms the adjective ‘of Maheśvara’; the feminine ई makes it the name of his Śakti. Vaiṣṇavī, Kaumārī and Nārasiṃhī are formed the same way.
A past participle standing for a finite verb (‘arrived’), the usual way these verses mark each arrival (8.20, 8.21).

mantras.anvaya: वृषारूढा त्रिशूलवरधारिणी महाहिवलया चन्द्ररेखाविभूषणा माहेश्वरी प्राप्ता।
mantras.anvaya_en: One subject (माहेश्वरी), four qualifying compounds, one verb (प्राप्ता).
mantras.lit: Māheśvarī, mounted on the bull, holding an excellent trident, with great serpents as bracelets, adorned with the crescent of the moon, arrived.
mantras.tr: Māheśvarī came, riding the bull and bearing a mighty trident, with great serpents for her bracelets and the crescent moon for her ornament.

comm.t: Śiva’s Śakti carries every mark of Śiva: the bull, the trident, the serpents and the crescent moon.
The gods praise her in the same form at 11.14 (त्रिशूलचन्द्राहिधरे महावृषभवाहिनि).
The Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has the name माहेश्वरी (name 208). There it names the supreme Goddess herself, not one Mother among seven.

morph.note: शक्ति here is Skanda’s weapon, the spear; the same word names the goddess as a ‘power’ (शक्तिः, 8.13). The verse plays on both.
Perfect of √या with two prefixes, अभि and आ: ‘came towards’ (the enemy).

mantras.anvaya: शक्तिहस्ता मयूरवरवाहना च गुहरूपिणी कौमारी अम्बिका दैत्यान् योद्धुम् अभ्याययौ।
mantras.anvaya_en: Subject (कौमारी, with अम्बिका in apposition and three qualifiers), infinitive of purpose with its object, verb.
mantras.lit: Kaumārī, spear in hand and with a splendid peacock as her vehicle, the Mother in the form of Guha, came forward to fight the Daityas.
mantras.tr: Kaumārī, spear in hand and riding a splendid peacock, came forward to fight the Daityas — the Mother in the form of Guha.

comm.t: Skanda’s Śakti has his spear and his peacock. She is called अम्बिका, ‘Mother’, the name the text otherwise gives to the Goddess herself: each Mother is the one Mother in another form.
The gods praise her at 11.15 as attended by peacock and cock and bearing the great spear (मयूरकुक्कुटवृते महाशक्तिधरे).

Vṛddhi derivative of विष्णु (वि → वै, u → av): ‘belonging to Viṣṇu’, with the feminine ई.

mantras.anvaya: तथा एव गरुडोपरि संस्थिता शङ्खचक्रगदाशार्ङ्गखड्गहस्ता वैष्णवी शक्तिः अभ्युपाययौ।
mantras.anvaya_en: Subject (वैष्णवी शक्तिः) with two qualifiers; one verb.
mantras.lit: Just so the Vaiṣṇavī Śakti, seated upon Garuḍa, with conch, discus, mace, Śārṅga and sword in her hands, came up.
mantras.tr: In the same way Viṣṇu’s Śakti, Vaiṣṇavī, came near, seated on Garuḍa, bearing conch, discus, mace, the bow Śārṅga and the sword.

comm.t: Viṣṇu’s Śakti rides his eagle Garuḍa and bears his five weapons, Śārṅga being the name of his bow.
The gods praise her at 11.16 with the same weapons (शङ्खचक्रगदाशार्ङ्गगृहीतपरमायुधे). Viṣṇu sends two more Śaktis, Vārāhī and Nārasiṃhī, from his avatāra forms (8.19–20).
The Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has the name वैष्णवी (name 892), there of the supreme Goddess. The two works are distinct.

samasa.sense: Viṣṇu’s Boar avatāra, whose body is the sacrifice
samasa.alt: Or a taddhita on the compound यज्ञवराह ‘the Sacrifice-Boar’: यज्ञवराहस्य इदम् ‘belonging to the Sacrificial Boar’. Either way it describes the form Hari bears.

morph.note: Present participle of √भृ (third class, reduplicated बिभर्-/बिभृ-). Reduplicating verbs have no nasal in the participle: बिभ्रत्, m. gen. sg. बिभ्रतः, f. बिभ्रती (next line).
Feminine of the vṛddhi adjective वाराह ‘of a boar’ (from वराह); with तनुम् ‘a boar’s body’. It is also the name the Śakti bears (Vārāhī, 8.49).
Perfect of आ + √या, as in 8.14.

mantras.anvaya: या अतुलं यज्ञवाराहं रूपं बिभ्रतः हरेः शक्तिः, सा अपि वाराहीं तनुं बिभ्रती तत्र आययौ।
mantras.anvaya_en: A relative clause (या … हरेः शक्तिः) identifies the subject; the main clause (सा अपि … आययौ) has the participle phrase वाराहीं तनुं बिभ्रती.
mantras.lit: She who was the Śakti of Hari, who bears the incomparable form of the Sacrificial Boar — she too came there, bearing a boar’s body.
mantras.tr: The Śakti of Hari — of him who takes the matchless form of the Sacrificial Boar — came there too, in the body of a boar.

comm.t: A second Śakti of Viṣṇu, from his Boar avatāra. The principle of 8.14 holds: as the god appears, so his Śakti.

In the Purāṇas the Boar who lifts the earth from the waters is the sacrifice embodied (yajña-varāha). The gods praise Vārāhī at 11.17 as the one who ‘raised up the earth with her tusk’ (दंष्ट्रोद्धृतवसुंधरे).

Vārāhī is also a warrior power in the Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa): name 76, विशुक्रप्राणहरणवाराहीवीर्यनन्दिता, ‘delighted by the valour of Vārāhī in taking Viśukra’s life’. The two battles are separate stories.

mantras.lit: Nārasiṃhī, bearing a body like that of Nṛsiṃha, arrived there — she by the tossing of whose mane the multitude of stars was scattered.
mantras.tr: Nārasiṃhī came there in a body like the Man-Lion’s, the tossing of her mane scattering the hosts of stars.

comm.t: The third Śakti from Viṣṇu, the power of the Man-Lion. The image of the mane scattering the stars gives her cosmic size.

The gods praise her at 11.18 as the one who, in the fierce Man-Lion form, set out to slay the Daityas (नृसिंहरूपेणोग्रेण हन्तुं दैत्यान् कृतोद्यमे). In the battle she tears the asuras with her claws (8.37).

mantras.anvaya: तथा एव वज्रहस्ता गजराजोपरि स्थिता सहस्रनयना ऐन्द्री प्राप्ता; यथा शक्रः, तथा एव सा।

mantras.lit: Just so Aindrī, thunderbolt in hand, standing upon the king of elephants, arrived, thousand-eyed: as Śakra is, exactly so is she.
mantras.tr: Aindrī came likewise, thunderbolt in hand, mounted on the king of elephants and thousand-eyed — in every way as Indra is.

comm.t: The last of the five gods’ Śaktis: Indra’s, with his thunderbolt, his elephant and his thousand eyes. The closing words restate the rule of 8.14: as the god, so his Śakti.
The gods praise her at 11.19 as crowned, bearing the great thunderbolt, shining with a thousand eyes, the slayer of Vṛtra (वृत्रप्राणहरे चैन्द्रि) — Indra’s own deed ascribed to his Śakti.

morph.note: Passive imperative: the passive stem हन्य- with the ātmanepada imperative ending -अन्ताम्. ‘Let the asuras be slain.’
A defective verb found only in a few forms (आह, आहुः …), perfect in its endings, ‘said’. It introduces direct speech; here the speech comes first and आह follows it.

mantras.anvaya: ततः ताभिः देवशक्तिभिः परिवृतः ईशानः चण्डिकाम् आह — “मम प्रीत्या असुराः शीघ्रं हन्यन्ताम्” (इति)।
mantras.anvaya_en: A main clause (ईशानः चण्डिकाम् आह) with the participle phrase परिवृतः … देवशक्तिभिः; the quoted request is a passive imperative.
mantras.lit: Then Īśāna, surrounded by those Śaktis of the gods, said to Caṇḍikā: “Let the asuras be slain quickly, for my pleasure.”
mantras.tr: Then Śiva, surrounded by those Śaktis of the gods, said to Caṇḍikā, “Let the asuras be slain at once, for my sake.”
mantras.tr_note: Īśāna is rendered as Śiva; मम प्रीत्या, ‘for my pleasure’, is rendered ‘for my sake’.

comm.t: Śiva (Īśāna) is on the field, among the Śaktis, and asks Caṇḍikā to destroy the asuras quickly. He does not fight; he asks.
Of the gods whose Śaktis came, only Śiva appears in person. His request opens the episode in which the Goddess sends him, of all the gods, on an errand (8.24–28).

samasa.sense: her cry is the howl of a pack of jackals
samasa.alt: Or a bahuvrīhi in sense, ‘she whose cry is that of a hundred jackals’; the meaning is the same.

morph.note: Past participle of वि + निस् + √क्रम् used as a finite verb: ‘came forth’. Kālī ‘came forth’ (विनिष्क्रान्ता) from the Goddess’s brow with the same word at 7.6.
शिवा (feminine) is the jackal, ‘the auspicious one’ by euphemism. The word prepares the name Śivadūtī (8.28) and the ‘jackals’ of 8.27.

mantras.anvaya: ततः तु देवीशरीरात् अतिभीषणा अत्युग्रा शिवाशतनिनादिनी चण्डिकाशक्तिः विनिष्क्रान्ता।
mantras.anvaya_en: Subject (चण्डिकाशक्तिः) with three qualifiers; source (देवीशरीरात्); verb (विनिष्क्रान्ता).
mantras.lit: Then from the Goddess’s body came forth the Śakti of Caṇḍikā, most terrible, exceedingly fierce, howling like a hundred jackals.
mantras.tr: Then from the body of the Goddess there came forth Caṇḍikā’s Śakti — most terrible, exceedingly fierce, howling like a hundred jackals.

comm.t: The gods have put forth their Śaktis; now the Goddess puts forth her own. She will be named Śivadūtī in 8.28.

Jackals haunt the battlefield and the cremation ground, and their howls are ill-omened. The Śakti’s jackal-cry marks her as a power of the battlefield; her terrible laughter again frightens the asuras at 9.23.

morph.note: Vocative, not a predicate: the nominative would be दूतः (दूतस्त्वम्). She addresses Śiva by his new office: ‘Messenger, go!’
Vocative of भगवत्, ‘O Blessed One’, with the strong stem’s n.

mantras.anvaya: अपराजिता सा च धूम्रजटिलम् ईशानम् आह — “भगवन्, दूत, त्वं शुम्भनिशुम्भयोः पार्श्वं गच्छ।”
mantras.anvaya_en: The narrative frame (सा … ईशानम् आह) and the start of her speech: two vocatives and an imperative with its goal.
mantras.lit: And she, the Unconquered, said to Īśāna, smoke-grey and matted-haired: “Messenger, go, O Lord, to the side of Śumbha and Niśumbha.
mantras.tr: And she, the Unconquered, said to the ash-grey, matted-haired Śiva: “Go, Lord, as my messenger to Śumbha and Niśumbha.
mantras.tr_note: The vocative दूत is rendered ‘as my messenger’; ‘my’ is supplied.

comm.t: The Goddess’s new Śakti makes Śiva himself her envoy to the asura kings. The speech runs to 8.27.

The scene reverses chapter 5, where Śumbha sent the asura Sugrīva as messenger to the Goddess (5.102). Now the Goddess sends the highest of the gods to Śumbha — in the Śākta reading, a sign that Śiva acts at the bidding of Śakti.

mantras.anvaya: अतिगर्वितौ दानवौ शुम्भं निशुम्भं च ब्रूहि, ये च अन्ये दानवाः तत्र युद्धाय समुपस्थिताः (तान् च ब्रूहि) —
mantras.anvaya_en: The imperative ब्रूहि with two named addressees; a relative clause adds the rest of the host, whose correlative (तान्) is understood.
mantras.lit: Say to Śumbha and Niśumbha, the two exceedingly proud Dānavas, and (to) the other Dānavas who are assembled there for battle:
mantras.tr: Say to Śumbha and Niśumbha, those two arrogant Dānavas, and to all the other Dānavas gathered there for battle:
mantras.tr_note: The correlative ‘to those’ is supplied for the relative clause.

comm.t: The message is addressed to the two kings and to the whole host. Its words follow in 8.26–27.
Like a royal embassy, the message is spoken to the rulers and their assembled vassals alike: it is an ultimatum, and all who hear it are bound by their answer.

samasa.sense: the gods restored to their share in the sacrifice

morph.note: A taddhita in -य with vṛddhi (त्रि → त्रै) on त्रिलोक: ‘the triad of worlds’, a collective neuter singular.
Third-person imperative, ātmanepada (√लभ् is ātmanepada): ‘let him obtain’.
√इष् forms its present stem इच्छ- (the root’s ṣ becomes cch): इच्छथ ‘you wish’.
भुज् is a root used as a noun at the end of a compound; consonant stem, nominative plural -अः.

mantras.anvaya: इन्द्रः त्रैलोक्यं लभताम्; देवाः हविर्भुजः सन्तु; यूयं यदि जीवितुम् इच्छथ, (तर्हि) पातालं प्रयात।
mantras.anvaya_en: Three imperatives: two third-person (for Indra and the gods), one second-person (for the asuras) with a conditional clause.
mantras.lit: Let Indra obtain the three worlds; let the gods be enjoyers of the oblations. You — go to Pātāla, if you wish to live.
mantras.tr: ‘Let Indra have the three worlds, and let the gods receive the sacrificial offerings. As for you, go down to Pātāla, if you wish to live.

comm.t: The terms of peace: Indra’s sovereignty and the gods’ share of the sacrifice are to be restored, and the asuras are to withdraw to the underworld.

The terms answer the wrong of 5.2, where Śumbha and Niśumbha took from Indra the three worlds and the shares of the sacrifice (त्रैलोक्यं यज्ञभागाश्च हृताः), and Śumbha’s boast at 5.108. They are fulfilled at the end of the war: the gods again enjoy their shares (12.34) and the surviving asuras go to Pātāla (12.35).

samasa.sense: out of arrogance in your might
the jackals that attend the Goddess’s Śakti

morph.note: Taken as the correlative of चेत् (‘if …, then …’). The joined text तदागच्छत can equally be read तदा आगच्छत, ‘then come’; the meaning is the same.
The honorific भवत् is grammatically third person, but the imperative that follows is second person (आगच्छत): the politeness of the address gives way to the challenge.
Enclitic form of the genitive plural of युष्मद् (= युष्माकम्); it never begins a sentence or pāda.

mantras.anvaya: अथ चेत् भवन्तः बलावलेपात् युद्धकाङ्क्षिणः, तत् आगच्छत; मच्छिवाः वः पिशितेन तृप्यन्तु।
mantras.anvaya_en: A conditional (चेत् …) with its main clause (तत् आगच्छत), and a closing imperative of the third person.
mantras.lit: But if, out of the haughtiness of strength, you are desirous of battle, then come; let my jackals be sated with your flesh.”
mantras.tr: But if, proud of your strength, you long for battle, then come — and let my jackals feast on your flesh.’

comm.t: The alternative to withdrawal: battle, and the asuras’ flesh for the jackals. The message closes with the jackals that marked this Śakti’s cry (8.23).

The charge of बलावलेप, arrogance in strength, is turned back on the Goddess by Śumbha at 10.3 (बलावलेपाद् दुष्टे त्वं मा दुर्गे गर्वमावह), where he accuses her of relying on others’ strength. Her answer there, that all these powers are her own (10.5), resolves both.

samasa.sense: the name given to Caṇḍikā’s Śakti for this deed
samasa.alt: Formally it could be a ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa, शिवस्य दूती ‘Śiva’s (female) messenger’; the verse’s own explanation (Śiva was made messenger by her) requires the bahuvrīhi.

morph.note: दौत्य, ‘the office of a दूत’, is a vṛddhi taddhita (दू → दौ). With नियुक्तः the office is put in the instrumental: ‘appointed with (= to) messengership’.
A bahuvrīhi in दूत takes the feminine ई when it names a woman: शिवदूती.
Past participle used as the finite verb, with ख्यातिम् as object: ‘she came to fame’.

mantras.anvaya: यतः तया देव्या शिवः स्वयं दौत्येन नियुक्तः, ततः सा अस्मिन् लोके “शिवदूती” इति ख्यातिम् आगता।
mantras.anvaya_en: A causal correlative: यतः (passive clause: शिवः … देव्या नियुक्तः) … ततः (सा … ख्यातिम् आगता).
mantras.lit: Because Śiva himself was appointed to the office of messenger by that Goddess, therefore she came to renown in this world as ‘Śivadūtī’.
mantras.tr: Because she made Śiva himself her messenger, the Goddess became known in this world as Śivadūtī — ‘she whose messenger is Śiva’.
mantras.tr_note: The passive is turned active, and the meaning of the name is added in apposition.

comm.t: The narrator explains the name: she is Śivadūtī because Śiva was her envoy. The formula follows the naming of Cāmuṇḍā (7.27: चामुण्डेति ततो लोके ख्याता).
Śivadūtī fights again in the next chapters (9.23, 9.37) and is praised in the hymn of chapter 11 (11.20: शिवदूतीस्वरूपेण हतदैत्यमहाबले).
The Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) also has the name शिवदूती (name 405). The shared name is a real point of contact between the two Śākta works.

mantras.anvaya: ते महासुराः अपि शर्वाख्यातं देव्याः वचः श्रुत्वा अमर्षापूरिताः (सन्तः), यत्र कात्यायनी स्थिता, (तत्र) जग्मुः।
mantras.anvaya_en: Subject (ते महासुराः) with an absolutive clause and a qualifier; main verb जग्मुः with a relative clause of place (यत्र … स्थिता).
mantras.lit: They, the great asuras, for their part, having heard the Goddess’s words announced by Śarva, filled with indignation, went where Kātyāyanī stood.
mantras.tr: And the great asuras, hearing the Goddess’s message as Śiva delivered it, went, seething with indignation, to where Kātyāyanī stood.

comm.t: The asuras reject the terms and march on the Goddess. Śiva is here called Śarva; the Goddess, Kātyāyanī.

As with the earlier messages (5.122 onward, 6.2), the answer to the Goddess’s word is indignation (अमर्ष) and attack. The tradition reads the pattern as the ego refusing the one offer that would save it.
The Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) has the name कात्यायनी (name 556). The two works share the name; their stories are separate.

mantras.lit: Then at the very first, in front, the enemies of the immortals, their indignation roused, rained upon that Goddess with showers of arrows, spears and swords.
mantras.tr: Then the enemies of the gods, their fury roused, at once rained down on the Goddess from the front showers of arrows, spears and swords.

comm.t: The asuras strike first, answering the message with a volley of missiles. ऋष्टि is a sword or two-edged blade; शक्ति here is the hurled spear.
The image of weapons as rain recurs in the next chapter, where Śumbha and Niśumbha pour arrows on the Goddess ‘like two clouds raining’ (9.9: मेघयोरिव वर्षतोः).

mantras.lit: And she, with great arrows loosed from her resounding bow, cut with ease those launched arrows, pikes, spears and axes.
mantras.tr: And with great arrows loosed from her thrumming bow she cut down, as if in play, the arrows, pikes, spears and axes they had hurled.

comm.t: The Goddess cuts every missile in the air. The word लीलया, ‘in play’, is the narrator’s mark of her ease.

The same word marks her battles in every carita: she cuts the weapons ‘as if in play’ at 2.50 and 3.4, and breaks Śumbha’s weapons so at 10.13 (लीलयैव). The tradition reads the divine acts of creation and destruction as her play (līlā).
The Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) gives the idea a cosmic scale: name 648, लीलाकॢप्तब्रह्माण्डमण्डला, ‘who fashioned the sphere of the universe in play’.

mantras.lit: Likewise Kālī then ranged in front of it, making the enemies torn by the blows of her spear and crushed by her khaṭvāṅga.
mantras.tr: So too Kālī ranged at the front of the fight, tearing the foe with blows of her spear and crushing them with her skull-staff.
mantras.tr_note: तस्य अग्रतः, ‘in front of it/him’, is rendered ‘at the front of the fight’; see the flag.

comm.t: Kālī fights in the van with spear and khaṭvāṅga. The Mothers’ deeds follow one by one (8.33–38).
The khaṭvāṅga was Kālī’s weapon from her first appearance (7.7: विचित्रखट्वाङ्गधरा), and the asuras fell to it then as now (7.15: खट्वाङ्गताडिताः).

flags.uncertain: तस्य is masculine or neuter: most naturally the enemy host (सैन्यम्), at whose front Kālī ranges, or Śiva, last named in 8.29. Many renderings take it as ‘before her (Caṇḍikā)’, which would need तस्याः; that reading treats the masculine as a licence.

Present with स्म: a present tense used for a past action, a regular Sanskrit idiom (the particle स्म turns the present into the past). येन येन स्म धावति: ‘wherever she ran’.
Accusative plural of the s-stem adjective हतौजस्; for s-stems the accusative plural has the same form as the nominative plural. It agrees with शत्रून्.

mantras.anvaya_en: Main clause ब्रह्माणी … शत्रून् … अकरोत् with two predicate accusatives; the relative clause येन येन धावति स्म says where.
mantras.lit: And Brahmāṇī, wherever she ran, made the enemies bereft of valour by the sprinkling of water from her water-pot, bereft of vigour.
mantras.tr: Wherever Brahmāṇī moved, she sprinkled the enemies with water from her water-pot and left them drained of valour and strength.
mantras.tr_note: The compound’s instrument (the sprinkled water) is turned into an action of Brahmāṇī; the sense is unchanged.

comm.t: The Mothers now fight, each with the emblem of the god she came from, as 8.14 announced. Brahmāṇī arrived carrying a rosary and a water-pot (8.15 साक्षसूत्रकमण्डलुः); her weapon is that water-pot. Her water does not wound; it takes the enemy’s strength away.

The hymn of chapter 11 remembers the same act: Brahmāṇī is praised there as the one who sprinkles water with kuśa grass (11.13 कौशाम्भःक्षरिके). The rite-implement of the creator becomes a weapon in the Goddess’s hand.

mantras.tr: Māheśvarī struck the Daityas down with her trident, Vaiṣṇavī with her discus, and Kaumārī, blazing with anger, with her spear.

comm.t: Three more Mothers fight, each with her god’s weapon: Śiva’s trident, Viṣṇu’s discus, Skanda’s spear (the śakti Kaumārī held in 8.17, शक्तिहस्ता).

The word शक्ति is used here in its weapon sense — the spear of Skanda — beside its other sense, ‘power’, in which the Mothers themselves are the gods’ śaktis (8.13). The text keeps both meanings in play.

mantras.tr: Torn apart by the strokes of Aindrī’s thunderbolt, Daityas and Dānavas fell to the earth in their hundreds, pouring out streams of blood.

The chapter 11 hymn praises Aindrī as the one with the great thunderbolt who took the life of Vṛtra (11.19 महावज्रे … वृत्रप्राणहरे). Her weapon is Indra’s, and so is her history.

samasa.alt: Or bahuvrīhi: वाराही मूर्तिः यस्याः सा, तया — ‘by her whose form is the boar’s’. Either way the agent is Vārāhī.

morph.note: Imperfect of नि + √पत्: the augment अ- stands between the prefix and the root (नि-अ-पतन्), so the prefix’s i turns to y.
A bahuvrīhi ending in the s-stem वक्षस् ‘chest’: nominative plural -वक्षसः, ‘(those) whose chests …’.

mantras.anvaya: वाराहमूर्त्या तुण्डप्रहारविध्वस्ताः दंष्ट्राग्रक्षतवक्षसः चक्रेण च विदारिताः (असुराः) न्यपतन्।
mantras.anvaya_en: The subject (the asuras) is understood; three descriptions in the nominative plural, all with the agent वाराहमूर्त्या, lead to the verb न्यपतन्.
mantras.lit: Shattered by blows of the snout, their chests wounded by the tips of the tusks, and torn apart by the discus, by the one in boar form, (the asuras) fell.
mantras.tr: Shattered by the blows of her snout, their chests gored by the tips of her tusks, torn apart by her discus, the asuras fell before Vārāhī.
mantras.tr_note: ‘Her’ is supplied: all three weapons are taken as Vārāhī’s (see Commentary).

comm.t: Vārāhī, who came in the form of the sacrificial Boar (8.19), fights as a boar: snout and tusks. The discus in the same sentence is most naturally hers too, though Vaiṣṇavī has just used a discus in 8.34.
The chapter 11 hymn gives the boar-formed Goddess a great discus and the tusk that lifted the earth (11.17 गृहीतोग्रमहाचक्रे दंष्ट्रोद्धृतवसुंधरे), which supports reading the discus here as Vārāhī’s.

Locative singular of the i-stem आजि ‘contest, battle’: -इ + locative → -औ.

mantras.anvaya: नादापूर्णदिगम्बरा नारसिंही च नखैः विदारितान् अन्यान् महासुरान् भक्षयन्ती आजौ चचार।
mantras.anvaya_en: Subject नारसिंही with her epithet; the participle phrase भक्षयन्ती with its object; the verb चचार with its place आजौ.
mantras.lit: And devouring other great asuras torn apart by her claws, Nārasiṃhī, who filled the quarters and the sky with her roar, roamed in the battle.
mantras.tr: Nārasiṃhī ranged over the field, filling the quarters and the sky with her roar, tearing other great asuras with her claws and devouring them.
mantras.tr_note: The participle विदारितान् (‘torn’) is rendered as a second action of Nārasiṃhī; the Sanskrit makes the asuras the object of one verb, भक्षयन्ती.

comm.t: Nārasiṃhī, who came in a body like the Man-Lion’s, scattering the stars with a toss of her mane (8.20), fights as a lion fights: with claws, teeth and roar. ‘Other’ (अन्यान्) sets her victims apart from those Vārāhī has just struck.

The chapter 11 hymn remembers her as the Goddess in the fierce Man-Lion form who set herself to kill the Daityas (11.18 नृसिंहरूपेणोग्रेण हन्तुं दैत्यान् कृतोद्यमे). Here, as in the hymn, she is named only by her form.

flags.uncertain: अन्यान् can also be read apart from विदारितान् — ‘(those) torn by her claws, and others too’, both devoured. The sense differs little; the reading of the text is not in doubt.

mantras.anvaya_en: Two clauses: the asuras fell; then she devoured them.
mantras.lit: The asuras, assailed by Śivadūtī with fierce loud laughs, fell on the earth; and then she at that time devoured them as they lay fallen.
mantras.tr: Struck down by Śivadūtī’s fierce peals of laughter, the asuras fell to the ground, and there she devoured them.

comm.t: Śivadūtī is the power that came out of Caṇḍikā’s own body with the cry of a hundred jackals (8.23) and sent Śiva as her messenger (8.28). Her weapon is her laughter: it fells the asuras, and she eats the fallen.
The same terrible laughter returns in the next battle (9.23 अट्टाट्टहासमशिवं शिवदूती चकार ह), and the hymn of chapter 11 salutes her as Śivadūtī who slew the mighty Daityas (11.20).

mantras.anvaya: इति क्रुद्धं महासुरान् मर्दयन्तं मातृगणं दृष्ट्वा देवारिसैनिकाः विविधैः अभ्युपायैः नेशुः।
mantras.lit: Seeing thus the band of Mothers, enraged, crushing the great asuras, the soldiers of the gods’ enemies vanished by various means.
mantras.tr: When they saw the furious band of Mothers crushing the great asuras, the soldiers of the gods’ enemies slipped away, each however he could.
mantras.tr_note: नेशुः is taken as ‘vanished, fled’ (see morph); ‘each however he could’ renders अभ्युपायैर्विविधैः.

comm.t: The rout of the common soldiers. The word for the Mothers is now collective — मातृगण, ‘the band of Mothers’ — and the asura rank and file disappear, as they will again in 9.41 (केचिद्विनेशुरसुराः केचिन्नष्टा महाहवात्).

flags.uncertain: नेशुः may also be rendered ‘perished (in various ways)’. The next verse speaks of the Daityas as ‘intent on flight’, so ‘vanished, fled’ is preferred.

morph.note: Present tense for a standing fact: ‘whenever a drop falls, an asura springs up’. The narrative pauses to state the rule of his nature.
The taddhita -तस् gives an indeclinable with ablative meaning: शरीरतः = शरीरात्, ‘from the body’.

mantras.anvaya: यदा अस्य शरीरतः रक्तबिन्दुः भूमौ पतति, तदा मेदिन्यां तत्प्रमाणः असुरः समुत्पतति।
mantras.anvaya_en: A यदा … तदा sentence in the present: condition and consequence.
mantras.lit: Whenever a drop of blood falls from his body to the ground, then an asura of his size springs up on the earth.
mantras.tr: Whenever a drop of his blood fell to the ground, an asura of his own stature sprang up from the earth.
mantras.tr_note: The Sanskrit present of general truth is rendered as a past, to keep the narrative tense.

comm.t: The verse states Raktabīja’s peculiar power: every drop of blood that reaches the earth becomes another asura his equal. The Devī Māhātmya gives the rule without explaining where it came from.

A modern reading: violence that only spills more of what it attacks multiplies it. The episode is often read today as a picture of habits and desires that grow each time they are fought on their own terms.

flags.uncertain: Variant (corrections.json): for the Gita Press तत्प्रमाणस्तदासुरः, GRETIL and Freund read तत्प्रमाणो महासुरः (‘a great asura of his size’). The Gita Press reading is kept; the sense is the same, only तदा (the correlative of यदा) is replaced by महा-.

mantras.tr: Struck by the thunderbolt, he bled at once and freely, and from that blood rose warriors with his form and his strength.

comm.t: The rule of 8.41 is now seen working: the first wound fills the field with Raktabīja’s doubles. ततः can be ‘then’ or ‘from it’; both fit, since the warriors rise from the blood.

mantras.anvaya: तान् सुरान् विषण्णान् दृष्ट्वा सत्वरा चण्डिका प्राह; (सा) कालीम् उवाच — चामुण्डे, वदनं विस्तीर्णं कुरु।
mantras.lit: Seeing those gods dejected, Caṇḍikā spoke in haste; she said to Kālī: ‘Cāmuṇḍā, make your mouth wide.’
mantras.tr: Seeing the gods in despair, Caṇḍikā spoke at once. She said to Kālī: ‘Cāmuṇḍā, open your mouth wide.’

comm.t: Caṇḍikā answers the gods’ fear with a plan, and the plan is Kālī’s mouth. She addresses Kālī by the name she gave her in 7.27, Cāmuṇḍā.
The hymn of chapter 11 salutes this form as Cāmuṇḍā of the terrible tusked mouth (11.21 दंष्ट्राकरालवदने … चामुण्डे मुण्डमथने). The wide mouth commanded here is the image the hymn remembers.

mantras.lit: With this swift mouth of yours, catch the drops of blood that arise from the fall of my weapons, and the great asuras (that arise) from a drop of blood.
mantras.tr: With this swift mouth of yours catch the drops of blood my weapons draw from him, and the great asuras born from those drops.
mantras.tr_note: ‘Those drops’ generalises the singular रक्तबिन्दोः ‘from a drop’.

mantras.tr_note: The sentence continues into 8.60.

mantras.anvaya: (देवी) चामुण्डापीतशोणितं तं रक्तबीजं जघान; शस्त्रसङ्घसमाहतः सः महीपृष्ठे पपात।
mantras.lit: (The Goddess) struck down that Raktabīja, whose blood had been drunk by Cāmuṇḍā. Struck by the mass of weapons, he fell on the surface of the earth,
mantras.tr: struck down Raktabīja, whose blood Cāmuṇḍā had drunk. Smitten by that host of weapons, he fell to the ground,
mantras.tr_note: The first line completes the sentence begun in 8.60; the second runs on into 8.62.

comm.t: The death of Raktabīja. Each detail matters: the blood had been drunk, so the many weapons that had multiplied him before now kill him.

mantras.anvaya: महीपाल, (सः) रक्तबीजः महासुरः नीरक्तः च (पपात)। नृप, ततः ते त्रिदशाः अतुलं हर्षम् अवापुः।
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line completes 8.61 (सः पपात); the second is a new sentence.
mantras.lit: — and bloodless, O protector of the earth, the great asura Raktabīja. Then those gods attained incomparable joy, O king.
mantras.tr: drained of his blood, O lord of the earth — Raktabīja, the great asura. Then the gods, O king, were filled with boundless joy.

comm.t: Medhas, the sage telling the story, addresses King Suratha twice (महीपाल, नृप), marking the turn of the episode. The gods, afraid in 8.52, now rejoice.

उद्धत is the past participle of उद् + √हन् (‘raised up’, hence ‘wild, unrestrained’). असृज् ‘blood’ is the same noun as in 8.52.

mantras.anvaya: तेषां (देवानां) जातः मातृगणः असृङ्मदोद्धतः ननर्त।
mantras.anvaya_en: A single clause; the genitive तेषाम् is taken with जातः.
mantras.lit: The band of Mothers born of them danced, wild with the intoxication of blood.
mantras.tr: And the band of Mothers born from the gods danced, wild with the blood they had drunk.
mantras.tr_note: ‘From the gods’ makes तेषाम् explicit; ‘they had drunk’ interprets असृङ्मद ‘intoxication of blood’.

comm.t: The chapter ends with the Mothers’ victory dance. तेषाम् recalls their origin: they came out of the bodies of the gods (8.13). This last mantra is a half-śloka; in recitation it carries the closing bīja ॐ, which belongs to the pāṭha, not to the verse.
The Mothers return to fight beside the Goddess in the next chapter (9.8 कृत्वा युद्धं तु मातृभिः) and are praised one by one in the hymn of chapter 11 (11.13–20).

flags.uncertain: तेषाम् could also be read with the whole clause (‘their band of Mothers’, i.e. the gods’ own), or as ‘among them (the gods)’. Taking it with जातः, ‘born of them’, agrees with 8.13.
